title: Kuku sibzamini
subtitle: Persian potato and herb frittata
excerpt: Kuku sibzamini is a Persian baked egg and potato cake, crispy on the outside and tender inside, flavoured with turmeric and spring onion. Unlike a standard frittata, it is cooked low and slow to build a dark crust on both sides and is served at room temperature sliced into wedges.
sourceNotes: Najmieh Batmanglij, Food of Life: Ancient Persian and Modern Iranian Cooking and Ceremonies (1986). Kuku sibzamini documented as a common home dish served at Nowruz (Persian New Year) alongside other kuku varieties. Margaret Shaida, The Legendary Cuisine of Persia (1992). Notes on the importance of the thick crust and slow cooking.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make up to a day ahead and serve at room temperature. Kuku is better not reheated.

content.text: Kuku sibzamini is a Persian potato egg cake: grated potatoes mixed with eggs, turmeric, and spring onion, cooked in olive oil in a frying pan until deeply golden and crispy on both sides. The potato cake is thicker and denser than a Spanish tortilla, and the crust is the point. It is served at room temperature, sliced into wedges, often as part of a spread.
Squeeze the grated {{potato}} very firmly in a clean cloth to remove as much moisture as possible. The drier the potato, the crisper the kuku.
Beat {{eggs}} in a large bowl with {{turmeric-ground}}, {{black-pepper}}, and {{sea-salt-fine}}. Add the squeezed potato, {{spring-onion}}, and {{plain-flour}}. Mix until well combined.

Heat {{olive-oil}} in a 26 cm non-stick frying pan over a medium heat. Pour in the potato mixture and press down into an even layer. Reduce the heat to medium-low. Cook for 20 minutes without disturbing until the base is deeply golden and the top is mostly set.

Slide the kuku onto a large plate, then flip it back into the pan uncooked side down. Cook for a further 15 minutes until the second side is also deeply golden. The kuku should be cooked through with no liquid egg in the centre.
Leave to rest for five minutes. Slide onto a board and cut into wedges. Serve warm or at room temperature.

items.symptom: The kuku is soggy rather than crispy
items.fix: Squeeze in a cloth until almost no liquid comes out. The excess moisture prevents the crust from forming.

items.cause: Pan not non-stick or not enough oil
items.fix: Use a good non-stick pan and do not attempt to flip until the base is properly golden and pulling away from the sides.

items.symptom: The centre is still runny after the second side cooks
items.fix: Press the mixture down to no more than 2 cm thick. A thicker cake will not cook through without burning the outside.

items.symptom: The kuku falls apart when cutting
items.cause: Not enough flour or not rested
items.fix: Measure the flour carefully. Let it rest for five minutes before cutting; it firms up as it cools.

content.text: Kuku is the Persian word for a baked egg cake or frittata, and there are many versions: sabzi kuku with fresh herbs is the most famous (eaten at Nowruz), but sibzamini (potato) kuku is perhaps the most everyday. It is a staple home cook dish, made for quick lunches and picnics, and is one of the things Iranians take on road trips or long journeys because it travels well at room temperature. The turmeric gives it a golden colour and warm flavour; the spring onion adds freshness. Served alongside mast-o musir and rice, it makes a simple and complete Iranian meal.
